lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- The Place Nobody Tells You About
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Luiza Sellmann | Lesson 10 -- The Place Nobody Tells You About

listenings.text: Right, you asked me for one place and I am going to give you three, which is what always happens when you ask me anything. There is a bakery on the corner which opens at six, and the woman whose name is on the sign still makes the coffee herself. Go before eight, because after that it is packed and the regulars who stand at the counter are not moving for anybody. Then there is the restaurant two streets down where nobody takes a reservation. That one is my go-to when I cannot decide, and the owner cooks one dish a day, so do not ask for a menu. And the bar on the corner is a hidden gem that everybody in my building swears by. Please do not put any of this on the internet.

Ana, quick one before the call. The venue we booked for November is the old factory in Barra Funda, which is the one you visited in March. The person who signs everything off is called Renata, and she is the only one who can approve a change to the layout, so anything that touches the floor plan goes through her. The team we are working with is the same crew that did the Adidas activation, which is good news, because they already know the building. And the insight from the last event, which is the part the client actually cares about, was that people stay much longer in a space that has a story. So keep the factory walls. Do not paint anything.

extra_audio.text: Nathan says he found a bakery which is empty at seven and packed by nine. Ana asks whether there was a woman whose name is on the sign. Nathan explains that she talked to him in Portuguese, which he does not speak. Nathan asks for somewhere to have dinner that is not full of tourists. Ana recommends the restaurant round the corner where nobody takes a reservation.

reading.rtitle: Brooklin on Foot -- Three Places the Locals Keep Quiet About
paras: There is a bakery on Rua Florida which opens at six in the morning and closes when the bread runs out. The people who work there have been behind that counter for twenty years, and the woman whose name is on the sign still makes the coffee herself.

The room is small, and on Saturdays it is packed. The regulars, who all know each other, stand at the counter and read the paper without saying much. If you want a table, the only time that works is before eight.

Two streets away there is a restaurant where nobody takes a reservation. It is the kind of place that people walk past for years without noticing, which is exactly why the food is still good. The owner, who moved here from Minas in the nineties, cooks one dish a day, and that is the menu.

And on the corner there is a bar which everybody in the neighbourhood swears by, mainly because of the man who works there on Fridays. It is a hidden gem, and the people who live on this street are not entirely happy that it is in this guide.
